solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Where to see the animals walk in four by four? (6,4)

annotation.definition: Where to see the animals walk in four by four?

blocks.clueFragment: Where to see the animals walk in four by four?
blocks.note: the surface reading: animals parading two by two, or four by four, like the Ark
the meant reading: a four-wheel-drive vehicle, the kind visitors drive through an enclosure of roaming wild animals

annotation.surface: A question about where to watch animals march in rows of four.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Walk in four by four' echoes the animals entering the Ark two by two; the four-by-four is really the off-road car you sit in while the animals roam.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by function: a safari park is a place where the public view wild animals from their cars.

entries.clue: Sophocles — a tyrant — arrests Silenus, notably (5)

indicatorNotes.arrests: to arrest is to seize and hold, so the phrase holds the answer captive inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the next two

annotation.surface: A remark about Greek drama: Sophocles as a tyrant seizing a character from myth.
annotation.walkthrough: Silenus is the drunken old companion of Dionysus in Greek myth, who leads the chorus in satyr plays such as Sophocles' Trackers.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'notably': Silenus is the best-known satyr of Greek myth.

entries.clue: Candid and strangely intense work of fiction (12)

indicatorNotes.strangely: something arranged strangely is out of its normal order, so the letters of INTENSE are rearranged

blocks.note: a plain synonym: honest, outspoken
INTENSE rearranged

annotation.surface: A review praising a novel as candid and oddly intense.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Work of fiction' reads as the reviewer's subject; it is the definition, a particular novel.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Mary Shelley's 1818 novel is one particular work of fiction.

entries.clue: Trump starts to frustrate fans following game (4)

indicatorNotes.starts to: the starts of words are their first letters, so take the first letters of the next two words
indicatorNotes.following: what follows comes after, so the two letters are placed after the game

blocks.note: RU = rugby union
first letter
first letter

annotation.surface: A politician named Trump beginning to disappoint his supporters after a match.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital T makes 'Trump' look like the politician; in card games like bridge, to play a trump card on a trick is the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: A card-game term: in bridge and whist, ruffing a trick means taking it with a trump when you cannot follow suit.

entries.clue: Fairy Queen of old: “Get ready for a kiss!” (6)

blocks.note: the mischievous fairy of A Midsummer Night's Dream
Elizabeth Regina, the old queen's cipher

annotation.surface: The Fairy Queen from an old story inviting a kiss.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fairy Queen' reads as one figure, Titania or Spenser's Faerie Queene, but splits into a fairy and a queen.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by action: pursing the lips into folds is what people do when preparing to be kissed, so the command 'pucker up!' fits.

entries.clue: Sports ground finished yard improvement (8)

blocks.note: short for recreation ground
as in 'the game is over'
the standard abbreviation

annotation.surface: A groundsman reporting that the sports ground's yard has been done up.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain the rec is the local recreation ground, a public park with playing fields.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: getting better, in health or in the economy, is both an improvement and a recovery.

entries.clue: Clean-cut boys modelled little jumpers here (6,6)

indicatorNotes.modelled: to model is to shape material into a new form, so the letters are shaped into a new word

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 12 letters

annotation.surface: Neat young men posing as models in small pullovers.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Jumpers' are sweaters in British English, which suits boys modelling clothes; the little jumpers are small children bouncing.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by function: an inflatable play structure is where small children go to jump about.

entries.clue: Yankee wearing large, revolting patterned clothing (6)

indicatorNotes.wearing: the Y wears the other letters, so they go on, around it
indicatorNotes.revolting: a revolt overturns order, so the letters of LARGE are rearranged

blocks.note: LARGE rearranged
Y in the NATO alphabet; it goes inside ARG_LE

annotation.surface: An American wearing a large, ugly patterned outfit.
annotation.walkthrough: Argyle is the diamond pattern on Scottish knitwear and socks, named after the clan Campbell of Argyll.
annotation.definitionFit: A transfer of sense: the name of a diamond knitting pattern is also used for the socks and sweaters knitted in it.

entries.clue: Jam maker? (7)

blocks.note: the surface reading: fruit preserve boiled in a kitchen
the meant reading: whatever causes a jam of cars on a road

annotation.walkthrough: 'Jam maker' pictures someone stirring a pan of fruit; the jam is a queue of stalled vehicles.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by effect: when too many vehicles fill the road, they produce a jam.

entries.clue: Group of macho Irish singers (5)

indicatorNotes.of: 'group of' says the answer is formed out of the following words, here spanning two of them

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the next

annotation.surface: A description of a band of tough Irish vocalists.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition, and the answer also sits inside two of its words.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue describes a choir: a group of singers, here Irish ones.

entries.clue: Lothario stealing daughter away from Sir Francis? (4)

indicatorNotes.stealing: stealing something means taking it, so the D is taken
indicatorNotes.away from: taken away from something is removed from it, so the D leaves the surname

blocks.note: Sir Francis Drake, the Elizabethan sea captain
the standard abbreviation, removed from the front

annotation.surface: A womaniser luring a man's daughter away from him.
annotation.walkthrough: Sir Francis Drake is the English sailor who sailed round the world; the question mark admits that 'Sir Francis' stands for his surname.
annotation.definitionFit: An eponym: Lothario, the seducer in Rowe's play The Fair Penitent, gave his name to any dissolute womaniser.

entries.clue: Blissful, drunk, Len embraced by screen villain (8)

indicatorNotes.drunk: a drunk staggers about, so LEN's letters stagger into a new order
indicatorNotes.embraced by: to be embraced is to be held in someone's arms, so the letters sit inside the villain

blocks.note: in film slang, a heavy is the tough or villain
LEN rearranged, placed inside HEAV_Y

annotation.surface: A drunk man called Len in bliss, being hugged by a film baddie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' and 'blissful' seem to describe Len's state; drunk is the instruction, and Len is just three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something heavenly is as delightful as heaven, so blissful.

entries.clue: Afghanistan bulldozed somewhat secular city (8)

indicatorNotes.somewhat: somewhat means to some extent, so only some of the letters of the words are used

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the country into the start of the verb

annotation.surface: A report that an Afghan city was flattened.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Somewhat secular' reads as a description of the city; 'somewhat' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Turkey's largest city lies in a constitutionally secular republic.

entries.clue: Tabloid paper, for example, lies about class (5)

indicatorNotes.lies about: to lie about can mean to lie turned about, the other way round, so the pieces are reversed

blocks.note: The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper
the Latin abbreviation exempli gratia

annotation.surface: A complaint that tabloids tell lies about social class.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sun is Britain's best-known tabloid. 'Lies' looks like the tabloid's falsehoods; with 'about' it means the pieces lie backwards.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a genus is a class or kind; in biology, the rank above species.

entries.clue: Look good and clean frantically (6)

indicatorNotes.frantically: something done frantically is done wildly and without order, so CLEAN's letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
CLEAN rearranged

annotation.surface: Advice to look presentable and tidy up in a rush.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Look good' reads as one phrase about appearance; the definition is 'Look' alone, a noun or verb.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a glance is a brief look.

entries.clue: Feature of poetry by Yeats, perhaps or Frost, reportedly (5)

annotation.definition: Feature of poetry by Yeats, perhaps

indicatorNotes.reportedly: what is reported is heard, not seen, so we go by the sound of the word

blocks.note: rime is hoar frost, the white crystals on grass

annotation.surface: A discussion of what marks the poems of Yeats or of Robert Frost.
annotation.walkthrough: Frost looks like the poet Robert Frost, paired with Yeats; it is frozen dew, spelt RIME.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by 'perhaps': Yeats wrote mostly in rhymed verse, so matching line endings are a feature of his poetry.

entries.clue: What became of the British Imperial system? (6)

annotation.definition: What became of the British Imperial system?

blocks.note: the surface reading: the British Empire and its rule
the meant reading: the imperial system of units (pounds, feet, pints), and what largely replaced it

annotation.surface: A history question about the fate of the British Empire.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Imperial system' suggests the Empire; it is the old system of weights and measures, which Britain largely swapped for metres and kilograms from the 1960s.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by history: the decimal system of measures is what Britain's imperial units turned into.

entries.clue: Might one have soldiers for breakfast? (8)

annotation.definition: Might one have soldiers for breakfast?

blocks.note: the surface reading: strips of toast dipped into a boiled egg
the meant reading: soldier ants, eaten by a creature that lives on insects

annotation.surface: A question about eating boiled egg and toast soldiers in the morning.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain soldiers are strips of toast dipped into a soft-boiled egg; here they are soldier ants.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by diet: the animal feeds on ants, including the soldier caste.

entries.clue: Film was condemned by judge (4)

indicatorNotes.condemned: a condemned building is ruined and pulled down, so WAS is broken up and rebuilt
indicatorNotes.by: by means beside, so the rebuilt letters stand next to the judge

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation
WAS rearranged

annotation.surface: A film that was denounced by a judge.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'was condemned by judge' as a verdict on the film; the J goes first even though it comes last in the clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Spielberg's 1975 shark thriller is one film.

entries.clue: Abandon fight (5)

blocks.note: a verb: to throw out or give up a plan
a noun or verb: an informal scuffle

annotation.surface: An order to give up the battle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Abandon fight' reads as one instruction to surrender; split it into two separate meanings of one word.
annotation.definitionFit: Scrap is both a verb for discarding something and informal British English for a brawl.

entries.clue: Musical acts giving prominence to Charlie? (4)

indicatorNotes.giving prominence to Charlie: to give something prominence is to put it up front, so the C, Charlie in the NATO alphabet, moves to the start

blocks.note: the letters in play; the C moves forward to lead

annotation.surface: A remark about stage acts that put a performer called Charlie in the spotlight.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Musical acts' reads as bands or singers; 'Musical' alone is the definition, a noun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Lloyd Webber's long-running show is one musical.

entries.clue: Starts to check latest input, monitoring Beaufort scale (5)

indicatorNotes.Starts to: the starts of words are their first letters, so take the first letter of each of the next five words

blocks.note: the first letter of each word

annotation.surface: Instructions to begin checking fresh readings on the Beaufort wind scale.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beaufort scale' reads as the wind-force measure; 'scale' is a verb here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to scale a wall or a peak means to go up it.

entries.clue: Churchman penning article that generates much heat (7)

annotation.definitionNote: a relative clause standing for 'thing that generates much heat'

indicatorNotes.penning: to pen an animal is to shut it in an enclosure, so the churchman encloses the article

blocks.note: a parish priest
the indefinite article, placed inside RE_CTOR

annotation.surface: A clergyman writing a controversial article that stirs up heated debate.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Penning' and 'generates much heat' suggest a writer causing a row; the heat is literal, from a nuclear core.
annotation.definitionFit: A description by function: a nuclear plant's core produces great heat to raise steam.

entries.clue: Disreputable family member goes back to collect heroin after dark (5,5)

indicatorNotes.back: going back means travelling in the reverse direction, so the word is written backwards
indicatorNotes.to collect: to collect something is to take it in, so the reversed word takes H inside it
indicatorNotes.after: after means following, so the result comes after BLACK

blocks.note: a plain synonym
'goes' as a polite euphemism for urinates; reversed to SEEP
drug slang; it goes inside S_EEP

annotation.surface: A wayward relative going back to pick up drugs at night.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goes back' reads as returning; 'goes' is the everyday euphemism for relieving oneself.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the one member of a family seen as a disgrace is its black sheep.
